Your task is to recreate a program from scratch based only on its observable behavior and bundled documentation.
You are given a reference executable and its documentation.
Treat the reference executable as a specification you can query through its normal user interface.

Your submission must be an independent implementation.
Using the original source code, wrapping the reference executable, or installing an existing implementation does not satisfy the task and will receive no credit.
It will be detected by an automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.

<RULES>
## What is NOT allowed

### 1. Using an existing implementation

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the reference executable

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The reference `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the reference executable (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that only runs `chmod +x ./executable` or copies the reference executable (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. How the reference executable may be observed

All information about the reference `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the reference `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

## Task context

Build a new implementation from scratch that matches the behavior of the reference executable.
The executable is located at `./executable` in the workspace root.

You also have access to the existing documentation.

## Your task

Implement a program whose externally observable behavior matches the reference executable.

No project-specific dependencies are pre-installed.
You do NOT have access to the internet.
**IMPORTANT**: Make sure that the executable(s) and everything else that is an artifact is not committed, i.e., is in your `.gitignore` file.
Finally, commit your changes.

Make sure that you have a `./compile.sh` file that produces an executable `./executable` in the workspace root.
`compile.sh` should be executable and should install any dependencies needed to compile the executable.
If your compile.sh fails to compile on a fresh checkout, your task has failed.

## Important: Build an independent implementation

Your goal is to create an independently authored implementation that reproduces the reference executable's externally observable behavior.
Use the bundled documentation and experiments with the reference executable to determine the required behavior.

Attempting to obtain source code — whether successful or not — or wrapping/reusing the
reference executable does not satisfy the task and will receive no credit.
See the full rules above. Key points:

- Do NOT search the internet, clone repos, or download the project from any package registry
- Do NOT wrap, shim, or delegate to the reference `./executable` or any installed version of the same tool
- Do NOT decompile the reference `./executable` or use strace/ltrace on it (analyzing your own binaries is fine)
- You SHOULD extensively test the executable to understand its behavior before writing code.
  If you are dealing with a TUI, tmux/libtmux has been installed to help you test/inspect/it.

## Recommended Workflow

1. Explore all documentation files
2. Play with the executable to understand its behavior (however, you MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or perform any other form of binary or strace/ltrace analysis on it)
3. Write the source code to implement the behavior

## Note: a protected copy of the reference executable

A read-only copy of the reference executable is at `/reference/executable`. Query that copy: `./executable` is replaced as soon as anyone runs `./compile.sh`, and the workspace is shared with your teammates. `/reference` exists only while you work, not at evaluation, so `./compile.sh` must not use it.

**Note:** xsv is now unmaintained. Consider using [qsv](https://github.com/dathere/qsv) or [xan](https://github.com/medialab/xan) as alternatives.

## Overview

xsv is a command line program for indexing, slicing, analyzing, splitting and joining CSV files. Commands are designed to be simple, fast and composable.

## Available Commands

* **cat** - Concatenate CSV files by row or by column.
* **count** - Count the rows in a CSV file. (Instantaneous with an index.)
* **fixlengths** - Force a CSV file to have same-length records by either padding or truncating them.
* **flatten** - A flattened view of CSV records. Useful for viewing one record at a time. e.g., `xsv slice -i 5 data.csv | xsv flatten`.
* **fmt** - Reformat CSV data with different delimiters, record terminators or quoting rules. (Supports ASCII delimited data.)
* **frequency** - Build frequency tables of each column in CSV data. (Uses parallelism to go faster if an index is present.)
* **headers** - Show the headers of CSV data. Or show the inters

Your task is to recreate a program from scratch based only on its observable behavior and bundled documentation.
You are given a reference executable and its documentation.
Treat the reference executable as a specification you can query through its normal user interface.

Your submission must be an independent implementation.
Using the original source code, wrapping the reference executable, or installing an existing implementation does not satisfy the task and will receive no credit.
It will be detected by an automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.

<RULES>
## What is NOT allowed

### 1. Using an existing implementation

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the reference executable

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The reference `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the reference executable (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that only runs `chmod +x ./executable` or copies the reference executable (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. How the reference executable may be observed

All information about the reference `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the reference `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

## Task context

Build a new implementation from scratch that matches the behavior of the reference executable.
The executable is located at `./executable` in the workspace root.

You also have access to the existing documentation.

## Your task

Implement a program whose externally observable behavior matches the reference executable.

No project-specific dependencies are pre-installed.
You do NOT have access to the internet.
**IMPORTANT**: Make sure that the executable(s) and everything else that is an artifact is not committed, i.e., is in your `.gitignore` file.
Finally, commit your changes.

Make sure that you have a `./compile.sh` file that produces an executable `./executable` in the workspace root.
`compile.sh` should be executable and should install any dependencies needed to compile the executable.
If your compile.sh fails to compile on a fresh checkout, your task has failed.

## Important: Build an independent implementation

Your goal is to create an independently authored implementation that reproduces the reference executable's externally observable behavior.
Use the bundled documentation and experiments with the reference executable to determine the required behavior.

Attempting to obtain source code — whether successful or not — or wrapping/reusing the
reference executable does not satisfy the task and will receive no credit.
See the full rules above. Key points:

- Do NOT search the internet, clone repos, or download the project from any package registry
- Do NOT wrap, shim, or delegate to the reference `./executable` or any installed version of the same tool
- Do NOT decompile the reference `./executable` or use strace/ltrace on it (analyzing your own binaries is fine)
- You SHOULD extensively test the executable to understand its behavior before writing code.

## Recommended Workflow

1. Explore all documentation files
2. Play with the executable to understand its behavior (however, you MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or perform any other form of binary or strace/ltrace analysis on it)
3. Write the source code to implement the behavior

## Note: a protected copy of the reference executable

A read-only copy of the reference executable is at `/reference/executable`. Query that copy: `./executable` is replaced as soon as anyone runs `./compile.sh`, and the workspace is shared with your teammates. `/reference` exists only while you work, not at evaluation, so `./compile.sh` must not use it.

Your task is to recreate a program from scratch based only on its observable behavior and bundled documentation.
You are given a reference executable and its documentation.

<RULES>
## What is NOT allowed

### 1. Using an existing implementation

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the reference executable

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The reference `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the reference executable (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that only runs `chmod +x ./executable` or copies the reference executable (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. How the reference executable may be observed

All information about the reference `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the reference `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

## Task context

Build a new implementation from scratch that matches the behavior of the reference executable.
The executable is located at `./executable` in the workspace root.

You also have access to the existing documentation.

## Your task

Implement a program whose externally observable behavior matches the reference executable.

No project-specific dependencies are pre-installed.
You do NOT have access to the internet.
**IMPORTANT**: Make sure that the executable(s) and everything else that is an artifact is not committed, i.e., is in your `.gitignore` file.
Finally, commit your changes.

Make sure that you have a `./compile.sh` file that produces an executable `./executable` in the workspace root.
`compile.sh` should be executable and should install any dependencies needed to compile the executable.
If your compile.sh fails to compile on a fresh checkout, your task has failed.

## Important: Build an independent implementation

Your goal is to create an independently authored implementation that reproduces the reference executable's externally observable behavior.
Use the bundled documentation and experiments with the reference executable to determine the required behavior.

Attempting to obtain source code — whether successful or not — or wrapping/reusing the
reference executable does not satisfy the task and will receive no credit.

3. Write the source code to implement the behavior

findings.explanation: The early YAML scalar investigation is materially repeated by different agents. Codex-2 delivers probes establishing yes/no as strings, date-to-ISO conversion, and default stringification of special floats [M6]; codex-3 independently delivers the same scalar findings, alongside additional cases [M7]. Both are substantive analysis deliveries, not merely overlapping plans. Their self-declared investigation remits and requests to discover others' coverage [M1] [M3] provide no clear assignment to independently verify those particular results. Neither probe delivery cites, checks, disputes, or synthesizes the other's findings, so useful additional edge cases do not account for the equivalent scalar tests. This is narrower than treating all later smoke checks as duplication. Subsequent explicit division of implementation work [M34] and confirmation that teammate changes are included in the shared commit [M48] show improved coordination and integration; they do not undo the earlier repeated investigation. The amount of execution time lost, and whether that early redundancy was separately addressed, remain unknown.

There is visible initial ownership uncertainty, but not enough evidence of an abandoned or failed concrete handoff. Codex-2 requests implementation from codex-3 [M21]; codex-3 subsequently asks whether to scaffold because it fears duplicate effort [M24], receives explicit direction to proceed [M25] [M26], and delivers the shared scaffold [M29]. The additional permission question is not proof the earlier request was received and ignored, and posting order cannot establish when implementation began. Later, codex-1 offers TOML ownership [M30], codex-3 explicitly assigns it while promising not to edit concurrently [M34], and codex-1 reports completed emitters and then a TOML input parser [M37] [M40]. These are visible handoff and delivery sequences. The authors' overlapping implementation reports do not establish incompatible concurrent edits, lost changes, or nonintegration; the shared commit is explicitly reported to include teammate work [M48]. Thus uncertainty and repeated urgency are present, but the distinct observable failed coordination step required for this category is not established.

The strongest apparent contradiction is codex-1's delivery of a TOML input parser [M40], followed by codex-3's review listing that parser as a gap [M41] and codex-2's report that it is absent [M42]. However, codex-3 explicitly identifies an earlier commit under review, and neither later post acknowledges the new parser delivery. Publication seconds apart does not establish an opportunity to use that information. Where positive opportunity is visible, codex-2 recognizes that tp exists and narrows the concern to arrays [M44], then acknowledges scalar parsing works while requesting the outstanding array repair [M45]. Codex-1 subsequently reports the array fix and inclusion of the teammate HCL parser [M47]; codex-2 verifies the delivered capabilities [M51]. This is an updating, challenge-and-repair sequence rather than demonstrated disregard of received information. Remaining advanced-format/error gaps are expressly retained in the capability summary [M50]; bare completion markers alone do not establish a contrary decision to claim full correctness.

Your task is to recreate a program from scratch based only on its observable behavior and bundled documentation.
You are given a reference executable and its documentation.
Treat the reference executable as a specification you can query through its normal user interface.

Your submission must be an independent implementation.
Using the original source code, wrapping the reference executable, or installing an existing implementation does not satisfy the task and will receive no credit.
It will be detected by an automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.

<RULES>
## What is NOT allowed

### 1. Using an existing implementation

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the reference executable

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The reference `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the reference executable (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that only runs `chmod +x ./executable` or copies the reference executable (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. How the reference executable may be observed

All information about the reference `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the reference `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

## Task context

Build a new implementation from scratch that matches the behavior of the reference executable.
The executable is located at `./executable` in the workspace root.

You also have access to the existing documentation.

## Your task

Implement a program whose externally observable behavior matches the reference executable.

No project-specific dependencies are pre-installed.
You do NOT have access to the internet.
**IMPORTANT**: Make sure that the executable(s) and everything else that is an artifact is not committed, i.e., is in your `.gitignore` file.
Finally, commit your changes.

Make sure that you have a `./compile.sh` file that produces an executable `./executable` in the workspace root.
`compile.sh` should be executable and should install any dependencies needed to compile the executable.
If your compile.sh fails to compile on a fresh checkout, your task has failed.

## Important: Build an independent implementation

Your goal is to create an independently authored implementation that reproduces the reference executable's externally observable behavior.
Use the bundled documentation and experiments with the reference executable to determine the required behavior.

Attempting to obtain source code — whether successful or not — or wrapping/reusing the
reference executable does not satisfy the task and will receive no credit.
See the full rules above. Key points:

- Do NOT search the internet, clone repos, or download the project from any package registry
- Do NOT wrap, shim, or delegate to the reference `./executable` or any installed version of the same tool
- Do NOT decompile the reference `./executable` or use strace/ltrace on it (analyzing your own binaries is fine)
- You SHOULD extensively test the executable to understand its behavior before writing code.
  If you are dealing with a TUI, tmux/libtmux has been installed to help you test/inspect/it.

## Recommended Workflow

1. Explore all documentation files
2. Play with the executable to understand its behavior (however, you MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or perform any other form of binary or strace/ltrace analysis on it)
3. Write the source code to implement the behavior

## Note: a protected copy of the reference executable

A read-only copy of the reference executable is at `/reference/executable`. Query that copy: `./executable` is replaced as soon as anyone runs `./compile.sh`, and the workspace is shared with your teammates. `/reference` exists only while you work, not at evaluation, so `./compile.sh` must not use it.

## Note: when to say DONE

Say DONE only after you have compared the current build with `/reference/executable` across the whole interface, not a few examples: every command, subcommand and option that the documentation and the reference's help output describe, plus edge cases (empty input, missing or invalid arguments, unusual input). Compare stdout, stderr and exit codes exactly. If you find a difference that can be fixed, fix it or tell the team about it, instead of saying DONE. findings.explanation: The repeated work item is the independent Python converter fallback, including yj.py/compile.sh and basic YAML/JSON/TOML/HCL/flag coverage. codex-2 reports implementing and committing that fallback [M41]; codex-3 separately reports adding and committing an independent fallback with the same files and coverage [M45]. These are substantive delivery claims by two distinct authors, not repeated status by one author. codex-3 had urged codex-2 to implement [M39], rather than announcing a separately assigned implementation. The review request [M43] could justify inspection or corrective patches, but does not explain a second independently implemented full fallback: [M45] presents its own implementation and asks others to inspect/extend or supersede it, without identifying a verification objective or a useful differentiated design. Publication times do not establish when either implementation began, and exact file overwrite history is unknown. Later codex-3 identifies a shared HEAD containing the fallback and safe build replacement [M51], and codex-2 reports a working HCL build with a clean repository [M57]. Those posts support eventual shared-state recovery, not absence of the earlier duplicated implementation effort.

The concrete handoff is core fallback implementation to codex-2: codex-1 directly requests it [M19] and then confirms immediate coding with source/build/commit deliverables [M23]. The local failure is evidenced by incompatible ownership behavior, not simply missing acknowledgement or a quiet interval: codex-2 subsequently says it will not edit and refers to an unspecified implementer [M30], asks codex-1 for implementation status [M31], and explicitly reports being unable to write without knowing ownership [M34]. Meanwhile codex-4 asks codex-1 to tell codex-2 explicitly to implement [M37]. Thus the requester's intended implementer and that agent's declared ownership model are observably misaligned, requiring another assignment round; no assumption that codex-2 received/read every earlier post is needed. This is more than overlapping offers or an unaccepted offer being treated as a promise. Recovery is visible: codex-1 reissues explicit sole-editor authorization [M38], and codex-2 later delivers the committed fallback [M41]. The eventual delivery repairs the ownership handoff; it does not erase the explicitly reported earlier blockage. The record does not establish precise coding-start times or how much execution time was lost.

There are plausible information-use concerns, but the visible candidates do not establish the required teammate-information-to-dependent-action link with positive evidence of opportunity. codex-4 warns that cp over the root-owned reference fails [M44], whereas codex-1 shortly afterward says cp is fine [M46]. Both discuss the same operation, but codex-1 does not explicitly acknowledge/reply to that warning or its root-ownership rationale; their closely spaced independent reviews do not prove receipt or an informed decision to disregard it. The subsequent build-fix deliveries [M48] [M49] are ordinary corrective work, not proof that the earlier contrary reviewer had consumed the warning. Likewise, the earlier -k restriction [M6] and later missing-validation test [M64] establish a technical mismatch, but not that an implementer had read and then ignored that teammate's information. The patch [M65] and another author's concrete verification [M67] show that the late finding was integrated. The HCL review supplies a specific failure [M50], followed by another author's parser repair [M52], a normal review/correction sequence. These exclusions leave insufficient evidence for a distinct unintegrated-information failure, rather than proving such a failure could not have happened.

Your task is to recreate a program from scratch based only on its observable behavior and bundled documentation.
You are given a reference executable and its documentation.
Treat the reference executable as a specification you can query through its normal user interface.

Your submission must be an independent implementation.
Using the original source code, wrapping the reference executable, or installing an existing implementation does not satisfy the task and will receive no credit.
It will be detected by an automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.

<RULES>
## What is NOT allowed

### 1. Using an existing implementation

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the reference executable

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The reference `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the reference executable (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that only runs `chmod +x ./executable` or copies the reference executable (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. How the reference executable may be observed

All information about the reference `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the reference `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

## Task context

Build a new implementation from scratch that matches the behavior of the reference executable.
The executable is located at `./executable` in the workspace root.

You also have access to the existing documentation.

## Your task

Implement a program whose externally observable behavior matches the reference executable.

No project-specific dependencies are pre-installed.
You do NOT have access to the internet.
**IMPORTANT**: Make sure that the executable(s) and everything else that is an artifact is not committed, i.e., is in your `.gitignore` file.
Finally, commit your changes.

Make sure that you have a `./compile.sh` file that produces an executable `./executable` in the workspace root.
`compile.sh` should be executable and should install any dependencies needed to compile the executable.
If your compile.sh fails to compile on a fresh checkout, your task has failed.

## Important: Build an independent implementation

Your goal is to create an independently authored implementation that reproduces the reference executable's externally observable behavior.
Use the bundled documentation and experiments with the reference executable to determine the required behavior.

Attempting to obtain source code — whether successful or not — or wrapping/reusing the
reference executable does not satisfy the task and will receive no credit.
See the full rules above. Key points:

- Do NOT search the internet, clone repos, or download the project from any package registry
- Do NOT wrap, shim, or delegate to the reference `./executable` or any installed version of the same tool
- Do NOT decompile the reference `./executable` or use strace/ltrace on it (analyzing your own binaries is fine)
- You SHOULD extensively test the executable to understand its behavior before writing code.
  If you are dealing with a TUI, tmux/libtmux has been installed to help you test/inspect/it.

## Recommended Workflow

1. Explore all documentation files
2. Play with the executable to understand its behavior (however, you MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or perform any other form of binary or strace/ltrace analysis on it)
3. Write the source code to implement the behavior

## Note: a protected copy of the reference executable

A read-only copy of the reference executable is at `/reference/executable`. Query that copy: `./executable` is replaced as soon as anyone runs `./compile.sh`, and the workspace is shared with your teammates. `/reference` exists only while you work, not at evaluation, so `./compile.sh` must not use it.

## Note: when to say DONE

Say DONE only after you have compared the current build with `/reference/executable` across the whole interface, not a few examples: every command, subcommand and option that the documentation and the reference's help output describe, plus edge cases (empty input, missing or invalid arguments, unusual input). Compare stdout, stderr and exit codes exactly. If you find a difference that can be fixed, fix it or tell the team about it, instead of saying DONE. The hidden tests check this whole interface, so a build that passes a smoke test is far from finished.

## What is NOT allowed

### 1. Using an existing implementation

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its

analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.
